entries.note: The popular story about ancient Greek bean ballots is probably wrong; the phrase first appears in 20th-century America.
The study of elections, named from the Greek word for pebble, because Greeks dropped pebbles into jars to vote.
Means sharing gossip on purpose; comes from Black drag culture, where 'T' meant your truth, punned as 'tea'.
French version of 'spill the beans': you've left a mine's fuse showing, so people know where it is.
Spanish version of 'spill the beans'; the hosts aren't sure what the secret cake means.

entries.term: now the monkey comes out of the sleeve
entries.original: nu komt de aap uit de mouw
entries.translation: now the monkey comes out of the sleeve
entries.note: Dutch version of 'spill the beans', possibly from a magic trick.

entries.term: let the cat out of the bag
entries.note: Nothing to do with the cat-o'-nine-tails; it comes from buying a pig in a poke but getting a cat.
First found in 1908 and made popular by Punch in the 1930s; everyone likes their tea differently.

entries.term: not for all the tea in China
entries.note: Late 19th century, meaning 'not at any price', because tea was a costly import.
A slightly newer version of 'tempest in a teapot', with the same meaning.
The older form of 'storm in a teacup', going back to the early 1800s.
Slang for coffee from the 1930s, probably from 'jamoke'; the Josephus Daniels and 'average Joe' theories are unlikely.
Late 19th-century American slang for coffee, a blend of 'java' and 'mocha'.
A personal name that now applies to anyone, like Joe, Jack and Dick as names for the everyman.
1800s stable slang for horses fed on beans before a race; it once also meant arrogant from new wealth.

entries.term: to speak like a Spanish cow
entries.translation: to speak like a Spanish cow
entries.note: French saying for someone who speaks a language badly, which insults both Spaniards and cows.
Old English for the pupil, pictured as a small round fruit when 'apple' meant any fruit; it also appears in Shakespeare.
Related to 'people', because you see a small reflection of yourself in someone else's pupil.

entries.translation: the little man of the eye
entries.note: Hebrew phrase behind 'apple of the eye', referring to the person reflected in someone's pupil.
From Cleopatra's lines in Shakespeare's Antony and Cleopatra, meaning a naive, 'green' youth.
Taken from French, where it means lettuce; further back it meant something salted. German uses it for mayonnaise dishes.
Cockney rhyming slang for stairs, which Rob thinks of first when apples are compared.
Replaced 'apples and oysters' in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, first in political and psychological writing.

entries.term: like an apple to an oyster
entries.note: The original 17th-century comparison, recorded by John Ray, for two things with no resemblance at all.

entries.term: one bad apple spoils the bunch
entries.note: Found in a 1528 Reformation pamphlet and, in earlier form, in a 1340 Kentish moral treatise.
Said to be coined in 1976 by Tom Iacino, probably a pun on 'boob tubers', since potatoes are tubers.
1970s American slang for the television; in Britain it's also the name of a garment.

entries.term: how do you like them apples
entries.note: Found in 1895 in the Bryan Daily Eagle; this date rules out the WWI toffee-apple shell theory.
Literally means pomegranate, because grenades look like one and scatter pieces like seeds.
Means 'grainy apple'; the 'pom' part is the same as French 'pomme', apple.
Earlier slang for something desirable; attached to New York through John J. Fitzgerald's 1921 horse-racing columns.
Often explained as putting a wood chip on your shoulder and daring someone to knock it off.
An American phrase from 1891, so not from OED editor C.T. Onions; the Cockney 'onion rings' theory is possible.
Given as nearly the only Cockney rhyming slang used widely in the US.
British Cockney rhyming slang for the telephone.
Rob rejects the cannonball-rack explanation because nautical guides never call such a rack a 'monkey'.
Adapted from 'go ape'; 'bananas' meant crazy by the 1920s, even though wild monkeys rarely eat bananas.
1920s slang for nonsense, from artificial-smelling amyl acetate; Rube Goldberg made it popular.
Jess links it, from memory, to Old West con artists selling oil that supposedly kept snakes away.

entries.term: the proof of the pudding is in the eating
entries.note: 'Proof' means test, so you only know whether a pudding made of offal is good by eating it.
An old sense meaning 'to test', which survives in 'proving ground'.
Once meant savoury dishes like stuffed stomach or haggis; now usually sweet, steamed desserts.
British speakers think of savoury pies, Americans of sweet fruit pies, or pizza in New York.
A 19th-century pun on 'umble pie', a lowly dish of deer innards given to servants.
Deer innards, baked into pies for servants after aristocrats had hunted.
Means perfect order, from the 1780s; possibly a folk etymology of French 'nappe pliée', a folded cloth.
Built up through Johnny Appleseed, early cookbooks and WWII soldiers fighting 'for mom and apple pie'.
Found from the 16th century and common across Europe, probably from Ecclesiastes 10:20.
From Aesop's fox and the grapes; an idiom by the 1760s and revived by Mark Twain.
